rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. This moderate-duration run establishes the critical pairs and a baseline for subsequent slope and temperature comparisons.

Only the first pair limits the score, so test a temperature-driven selectivity change while keeping the gradient fixed. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, preserving room to flatten the gradient if needed.
Lengthen the gradient one step at 60 C to try to raise the first pair from R 1.41 to at least 1.5. The last peak at 6.56 minutes leaves ample margin below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a shorter method while preserving full resolution. This gradient is only slightly steeper than injection 3 and ends above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction, so it should shorten retention while keeping the critical pair near or above R 1.5.

Shorten the programmed gradient to 8 minutes while increasing its slope only slightly, targeting a modest retention-time reduction without losing full resolution. The final organic fraction remains above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction of about 0.57.

Shift the gradient window upward by 0.05 while keeping its slope fixed to test whether retention can be shortened without sacrificing the first pair. Injection 5 remains a fully resolved fallback if the higher starting organic fraction reduces selectivity.

Restore the lower starting organic fraction and test a slightly steeper, shorter gradient, targeting first-pair resolution just above 1.5. The last peak may elute briefly into the final hold, but its estimated elution fraction is close to 0.55, making this a reasonable test for a shorter fully resolved method.

Test a small slope increase from 0.0833 to 0.085 organic fraction per minute to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary. Extending the gradient beyond the last peak also avoids the final-hold broadening seen in injection 7; that method remains the best shorter fully resolved fallback.

Test whether a shallower gradient restores the first-pair resolution lost at the higher starting organic fraction in injection 6. This combination may retain the time savings from starting at 0.10 while reaching full resolution; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Reduce the slope to 0.070 per minute to test whether the first pair reaches R ≥ 1.5 at the higher starting fraction. This completes the local resolution-boundary check while preserving injection 7 as the fastest fully resolved method observed.

With the maximum CRF secured, probe the low-temperature endpoint for an alternative selectivity regime, including possible elution-order changes. The broad gradient limits the risk of missing late compounds, while injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Test whether a substantially steeper gradient separates the late three-peak cluster through slope-dependent selectivity while shortening the low-temperature run. Keeping temperature and endpoints fixed isolates the slope response; the first pair’s R 2.58 provides some margin for compression.

The late cluster barely responds to slope, so raise temperature to change its selectivity while retaining a relatively short gradient. This tests the lower-temperature region where the first pair may remain resolved before its near-coelution around 40 C.

Test a higher starting fraction at 35 C to shorten the low-temperature branch while moving the late cluster away from coelution. The window shift also probes whether first-pair selectivity can support a faster fully resolved method than the current 60 C optimum.

Lower the starting organic fraction and flatten the gradient to improve the first pair at 35 C, where the late cluster is already resolved. This tests a fully resolved lower-temperature alternative while retaining injection 7 as the fastest proven method.

Test whether a substantially higher starting fraction changes first-pair selectivity enough to enable a faster low-temperature method. This also checks the onset of weak retention; the proven CRF 1.000 methods remain available if early peaks become compressed.

Return to a low starting fraction and slightly flatten the gradient relative to injection 15 to bring its first pair above R 1.5. The higher endpoint should keep the last peak inside the gradient, testing a fully resolved lower-temperature alternative below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Use a slope of 0.0708 per minute to recover full first-pair resolution at 35 C, while the higher starting fraction should bring the last peak below 10 minutes compared with injection 17. This targets a maximum-score lower-temperature alternative; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Return to the faster 60 C regime and trim injection 3’s gradient window while preserving its slope and expected R 1.67 minimum resolution. This targets the same maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient and more resolution margin than injection 7.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a shallower gradient for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Monitor both the first pair, which improves with shallower slope, and the third–fourth pair, whose resolution has been decreasing.

Use some of injection 20’s resolution margin to shorten retention by raising the starting fraction and slightly steepening the gradient. This should provide an intermediate option between the fastest fully resolved method and the higher-margin method, with the last peak expected near 8 minutes.

Refine the higher-starting-fraction resolution boundary with a slope of 0.0708 per minute, just steeper than injection 10. This may slightly shorten its retention while preserving R ≥ 1.5; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Shorten the higher-margin method from injection 20 by narrowing the window and slightly increasing the slope, targeting full resolution with the last peak around 8.6 minutes. This tests a shorter alternative with more resolution margin than injection 7, which remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 23 to shorten retention while retaining an estimated minimum resolution near 1.8. This refines the time–resolution tradeoff among maximum-score methods; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Test a six-minute gradient with the same slope as injection 19, targeting its R 1.67 resolution margin with a shorter programmed gradient. The last peak will likely elute during the hold but should remain below 10 minutes; injection 7 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.
